newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar finishes 1996 Tokyo up, but off day's high.
newsitem.headline: Dollar finishes 1996 Tokyo up, but off day's high.

text.p: 0630 GMT 2400 GMT NYK CLOSE

The dollar was standing at its highest level in 45 months in Tokyo against the yen on the last trading day of the year here, but failed to break above the high of 116.20 set in Friday's New York trade.
Carrying over the bullish sentiment from last week, and helped further by commercial buying, the dollar managed to rise as high as 116.18 yen before succumbing to profit-talking.
With participation limited ahead of the New Year holidays and no fresh incentives around, the dollar was merely moving along its recent bullish path, dealers said.
The continued weakness in Japanese financial markets also gave dealers assurance in buying the dollar, they said.
The key Nikkei 225 stock index ended the final session of 1996 down 7.69 points or 0.04 percent at 19,361.35, after falling as low as 19,108.50.
But the greenback failed to climb above 116.20 yen as dealers were not inspired to try the topside and were content to take profits just below the New York high, they added.
"At this time of the year, why try anything new? Conventional wisdom tells you to take profits at the highs," said a dealer with a European bank in Tokyo.
Japan's currency market closes for the year at 0900 GMT. Trade will resume on January 6.

Some dealers also said very small sales by exporters were detected at the highs, although other dealers said exporters had left sales orders placed at 116.30 and 116.50 yen prior to starting their holidays.
Movements in the dollar/mark arena were directionless, following in the footsteps of dollar/yen trade, dealers said.
Some Singapore dealers said rumours of a European central bank offering to sell at 1.5600 marks capped the dollar.
Most Tokyo dealers said they expect the dollar to head higher in the New Year, buoyed by a battered yen.

Weakness in Tokyo share prices has strengthened the view that Japan will be forced to keep its interest rates at record lows, leaving the yen less attractive than currencies with higher yields such as the dollar.
Apart from frail stocks, a recent sell-off of yen bonds has aroused concerns of a "triple weakness", in which the yen is sold as capital flows out of Japanese stocks and bonds.
In addition, many participants do not expect monetary authorities to voice concern over the dollar's rise during the holiday period.
"I don't think authorities, especially those in Japan, will be able to intervene even verbally ahead of the G7 meeting," said a trust bank dealer.

The next meeting of finance ministers and central bankers of the Group of Seven (G7) nations is widely expeted to be held in late January or February. -- Jacqueline Wong, Singapore Newsroom (65 870 3088) -- George Nishiyama, Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-5473-3710
